lines: Morgan Kim
+1 (555) 010-8173 | morgan.kim@example.com | example.com/code/mkim
EDUCATION
Clearwater Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2017 - May 2021
EXPERIENCE
Clearwater Sensors | Hardware Test Engineer | Metro City, USA | Apr 2022 - Feb 2023
- Automated end-of-line tests for a humidity sensor, cutting test time per unit from 90 to 25 seconds across 20,000 units a month.
- Traced a batch of early field failures to a solder-paste change; the findings updated the reflow profile and cut returns from 2.1% to 0.4%.
- Wrote the calibration procedure for the sensor line, cutting calibration drift complaints from 15 to 2 a quarter.
- Designed a test fixture that checked 8 boards at once, raising station throughput from 40 to 150 boards an hour.
Voltline Robotics | Embedded Software Engineer | Metro City, USA | Mar 2023 - Jun 2025
- Improved update speed by 60% by compressing firmware images and resuming interrupted downloads.
- Wrote a hardware-in-the-loop test rig that ran 400 motor-control tests on every firmware build.
- Added a crash logger that saved the last 2 seconds of sensor data to flash, which found the root cause of 5 field failures.
- Sampled the motor's 5 kHz vibration signal at 8 kHz so the fault detector could capture it without aliasing.
- Fixed a race condition on the counter shared by the interrupt handler and the main loop by declaring the counter volatile.
- Rewrote the motor-controller firmware for a warehouse robot fleet of 300 units, cutting control-loop jitter from 120 to 15 microseconds and field motor faults by 60%.
PROJECTS
Low-Power Weather Station | Independent Project | C, STM32 | Jan 2025 - Present
- Engineered a next-generation, innovation-driven IoT solution that redefines sustainable environmental sensing.
- Cut average current from 4.2 mA to 0.9 mA by sleeping between readings and batching radio transmissions.
- Published the schematics and firmware openly, and a local school built two stations from them.
Formula Student Electric Car | Electronics Lead, Team of 12 | C | Sep 2019 - May 2021
- Worked on firmware and testing for the robot fleet's motor controllers.
- The CAN-bus firmware for the dashboard was written and tested against the motor controller before each race.
- Rewrote motor-control firmware for a fleet of about 300 robots, cutting control-loop jitter eightfold and motor faults by more than half.
SKILLS
Tools: C, C++, STM32, oscilloscopes
Methods: firmware, hardware-in-the-loop testing, CAN, low-power design

items.says: Make the code URL complete and clickable.
items.because: A bare or incomplete-looking URL creates unnecessary friction for recruiters.

items.says: Ensure the linked profile or repository is polished, relevant, and publicly accessible.
items.because: Recruiters often check links quickly.

items.says: Consider adding a LinkedIn URL if it is complete and current.
Use a consistent location and date structure throughout the résumé.
items.because: Education should be easy to scan and should not compete with professional work.

items.says: Consider putting the degree before the school.
items.because: That may better support quick scanning.

items.says: Clarify what kind of time the automation reduced.
items.because: “Test time per unit” could mean test duration, operator time, cycle time, or total production time.

items.says: Clarify whether 20,000 units a month were directly affected by the automation.
items.because: The figure could instead be the line’s general output.

items.says: Clarify who implemented the reflow-profile change.
items.because: The wording should not imply you alone made a change performed by another team.

items.says: Add the time period or number of units behind the return-rate comparison if available.
items.because: The comparison needs statistical context.

items.says: Specify what the calibration drift complaints were.
items.because: Their source and definition matter for credibility.

items.says: Clarify that both quarterly complaint counts cover comparable periods.
items.because: The before-and-after measurement needs a consistent basis.

items.says: Consider a verb stronger than “wrote” if you also validated or implemented the procedure.
items.because: “Wrote” may understate broader ownership.

items.says: Clarify whether throughput was measured at the station level and whether other changes contributed.
items.because: Staffing or process changes could have affected the result.

items.says: Name relevant technical features of the fixture if space allows.
items.because: More technical detail would distinguish the engineering work from a simple process change.

items.says: Define what “update speed” measures.
items.because: It could mean elapsed update time, download throughput, deployment time, or fleet rollout time.

items.says: Identify the update mechanism or communication path if relevant.
items.because: Embedded hiring managers will want to know which part of the process improved.

items.says: Ensure the 60% improvement compares like conditions.
Add an outcome from the hardware-in-the-loop rig if available.
items.because: The bullet emphasizes activity and test count rather than value produced.

items.says: Clarify whether the rig ran automatically in CI or only locally.
Clarify whether the logger used a rolling buffer and preserved data through resets or power loss, if relevant.
items.because: Those details would explain the system design.

items.says: Clarify whether the logger directly resolved five failures or merely helped investigate them.
items.because: The claimed field impact depends on that distinction.

items.says: Sampling a 5 kHz signal at 8 kHz cannot capture it without aliasing as claimed.
items.because: The basic Nyquist criterion requires a sampling rate above 10 kHz.

items.says: Declaring a shared counter `volatile` alone does not fix a race condition.
items.because: `volatile` does not provide atomicity or mutual exclusion.

items.says: Clarify whether you led or substantially performed the firmware rewrite.
items.because: The bullet claims substantial ownership.

items.says: Define what “field motor faults” measures.
items.because: It could mean a fault rate, incident count, or service events.

items.says: Verify the 300-unit scale and improvements are attributable to this work.
items.because: The same achievement appears in the Formula Student project, creating a credibility problem.

items.says: Remove the promotional weather-station bullet.
items.because: It is vague and unsupported by technical detail, while the other bullets show value more convincingly.

items.says: Clarify the current-measurement conditions and use the same workload and method for both figures.
items.because: Sampling interval, radio technology, operating mode, or measurement duration could materially affect the result.

items.says: Clarify that the school built functioning stations from the published materials.
items.because: That would make the contribution and validation clear.

items.says: Mention deployment or instructional use if it adds meaningful evidence.
items.because: That context could better establish real-world use.

items.says: Ensure the claim that the materials were published openly is backed by a visible repository.
Replace “Worked on” with a specific responsibility.
items.because: The wording is too vague.

items.says: A robot fleet appears inconsistent with a Formula Student electric-car project.
items.because: The bullet sounds copied from professional experience and calls the project’s accuracy into question.

items.says: Replace any overlap with the Voltline job with a project-specific contribution.
items.because: The current bullet sounds copied from the professional experience section.

items.says: State whether you wrote the dashboard firmware, tested it, or both.
items.because: The passive construction makes your role unclear.

items.says: Explain what testing the dashboard firmware against the motor controller involved.
items.because: The technical scope of the pre-race testing is unclear.

items.says: Use consistent capitalization and terminology for CAN throughout the résumé.
The 300-robot firmware achievement is misplaced and duplicates the Voltline accomplishment.
items.because: A Formula Student car is not a fleet of warehouse robots, and the project predates the Voltline role.

items.says: Reorganize the “Tools” category by skill type.
items.because: It mixes languages, a microcontroller platform, and test equipment.

items.says: Broaden the skills list with relevant technologies you can discuss in an interview.
items.because: The current list undersells you and omits technologies implied by the experience bullets.

items.says: Reorganize the “Methods” category by skill type.
items.because: It mixes a discipline, a protocol, a testing approach, and an engineering specialty, making the section harder to scan.

items.says: Consider reducing the projects section and keeping Formula Student only with accurate, project-specific contributions.
items.because: With more than three years of relevant professional experience, projects should support rather than compete with the work history.

items.says: Make the independent project’s overlapping dates and “Present” label clear and accurate.
items.because: The overlap is normal for a side project, but “Present” should match the résumé’s submission date.
